rubric_v1_gloss: “To insist that you know it all, that everything be done your way, snatching from others and appropriating for your own use—this is called avarice.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 four evils (Watson tr.): appropriating others’ affairs, not merely money.

teaching.quote: … To insist that you know it all, that everything be done your way, snatching from others and appropriating for your own use—this is called avarice. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The fault overlaps with officiousness, but here the marker is controlling and appropriating.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To be fond of plunging into great undertakings, altering and departing from the old accepted ways, hoping thereby to enhance your merit and fame—this is called avidity.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 four evils besetting undertakings (Watson tr.), with the stranger’s role critique.

teaching.quote: “As for the four evils that I spoke of, to be fond of plunging into great undertakings, altering and departing from the old accepted ways, hoping thereby to enhance your merit and fame—this is called avidity. … If you do away with the eight faults and avoid committing the four evils, then and only then will you become capable of being taught!”
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: Not all change is avidity. The fame aim is part of the definition.

rubric_v1_gloss: “When men agree with you, to commend them; when they disagree with you, to refuse to see any goodness in them even when it is there—this is called bigotry.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 four evils (Watson tr.): agreement-based evaluation.

teaching.quote: … When men agree with you, to commend them; when they disagree with you, to refuse to see any goodness in them even when it is there—this is called bigotry. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The fault is not limited to religious hostility. It requires that goodness actually be present and be denied because of disagreement.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To see your errors but refuse to change, to listen to remonstrance but go on behaving worse than before—this is called obstinacy.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 four evils (Watson tr.), and Confucius’s response in the chapter.

teaching.quote: … To see your errors but refuse to change, to listen to remonstrance but go on behaving worse than before—this is called obstinacy. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

teaching.quote: … “I am aware of no error of my own, and yet why did I fall victim to these four persecutions?” … Confucius once more bowed twice, straightened up, and said, … “I would like to be allowed to go there, receive instruction, and at last learn the Great Way!”
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: Disagreeing with a remonstrance one judges mistaken is not shown by the source to be obstinacy. The source leaves this case open.
